target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society overall because it offers convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace-safety benefits.
objection: AI creates serious privacy harms, undermines critical thinking, intensifies racial discrimination, and harms economic well-being; these harms are presented as persisting alongside the benefits, so the benefits do not outweigh them.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI’s privacy harms will remain severe and society-wide in well-governed uses.
objection: There are practical technical and organizational safeguards—such as data minimization, access controls, auditing, and privacy-preserving methods—that can substantially reduce privacy risks in well-governed deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably or persistently exacerbates racial discrimination.
objection: Bias testing, dataset auditing, and fairness-oriented model adjustments can substantially reduce discriminatory outcomes, so racial discrimination need not persist when mitigation is implemented.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily undermines critical thinking in education and decision-making.
objection: AI can be used as educational support—through tutoring, feedback, and learning assistance—in ways that preserve or even strengthen reasoning rather than replacing it.

target: AG2’s conclusion that AI’s harms outweigh its benefits across relevant settings.
objection: If major harms such as privacy, discrimination, and education-quality degradation can be substantially reduced in well-governed deployments, then there is not clear evidence that AI’s harms outweigh its benefits overall.

target: AG1’s reliance on a “well-governed deployments” model to defend AI.
objection: AI is usually deployed by competitive, profit-driven organizations that have strong incentives to expand data collection and cut compliance costs, making strict safeguards difficult to sustain in practice.

target: AG1’s assumption that well-governed deployments are representative of real-world AI use.
objection: Because the incentives described make sustained governance hard, the “well-governed deployment” scenario is not generally representative of relevant real-world settings.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy and racial-harm safeguards are absent in real deployments.
objection: Legal, regulatory, and market incentives push AI providers to implement privacy and discrimination safeguards, so many real-world deployments do include access controls, monitoring, auditing, and fairness testing.

target: AG2’s claim that severe privacy and discriminatory harms are inevitable in realistic AI deployment.
objection: If safeguards are maintained to a meaningful degree, the most severe society-wide privacy and discriminatory harms are not inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy and anti-discrimination safeguards address the main harms of AI.
objection: Even when privacy and discrimination safeguards are maintained, AI can still undermine critical thinking skills for students and adults.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy and anti-discrimination safeguards prevent AI from being socially harmful.
objection: AI can still harm the economic well-being of many people and businesses even when privacy and discrimination safeguards are in place.

target: AG1’s inference that social benefits plus some safeguards establish an overall net positive.
objection: If critical-thinking harms and economic harms persist regardless of privacy and discrimination safeguards, then convenience, health, accessibility, and safety benefits do not by themselves show AI is overall net positive.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is net negative overall despite workplace-safety and accessibility benefits.
objection: AI can improve worker safety, reduce injuries, and improve workers’ well-being, which in turn reduces medical burdens and lost work time and can offset some economic harm.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI’s workplace-safety benefits do not help marginalized groups or overall welfare.
objection: AI accessibility features can expand participation for people with disabilities, increasing inclusion and social welfare and mitigating economic and social exclusion harms.

target: AG1’s workplace-safety argument that AI only needs environmental data and not worker tracking.
objection: Workplace-safety AI often requires detailed worker information such as location, activity traces, sensor logs, and other identifying data, so safety AI commonly creates privacy risks for workers.

target: AG1’s claim that workplace-safety AI does not create serious privacy harm if it improves safety.
objection: Even when safety monitoring reduces injuries, it can still invade workers’ privacy and cause harms like loss of autonomy and data misuse.

target: AG1’s claim that workplace AI for safety does not contribute to economic harm.
objection: Workplace AI can also intensify automation and management pressures, contributing to economic instability and livelihood harm for workers.

target: AG1’s claim that safety and accessibility benefits offset AI’s harms in workplace deployments.
objection: Privacy harms and economic harms can persist even when some injuries are reduced, so safety and accessibility benefits do not reliably offset those harms.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace-safety AI necessarily requires detailed worker-identifying traces.
objection: Safety AI can be implemented using environmental and asset signals—such as machine state, vibration, temperature, chemical sensors, and hazard zones—without tracking worker identity or detailed location/activity traces.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace-safety AI inevitably causes serious privacy harms to workers.
objection: If safety AI uses mainly environmental signals rather than detailed worker traces, the serious privacy harms associated with surveillance and misuse are substantially reduced.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace-safety AI is net harmful overall.
objection: When safety AI reduces accidents and injuries and serious privacy harms are substantially reduced through privacy-preserving design, workplace-safety deployments need not be overall net negative.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace-safety and accessibility benefits fail to offset broader harms.
objection: Workplace safety AI reduces injury-related costs and lost work time, and accessibility AI increases participation for marginalized groups, so these benefits can offset key economic and social harms.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s benefits do not produce overall net positive social welfare in realistic deployments.
objection: Because AI can improve safety, accessibility, and social participation while reducing injuries and exclusion, it can still be good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that safety-focused AI inevitably causes economic instability.
objection: Safety-focused AI can be limited to hazard detection and incident prevention without being used for labor replacement or cost-intensifying workforce management, so economic instability is not inevitable.

target: AG2’s claim that safety and inclusion benefits cannot outweigh harms.
objection: If safety-focused AI reliably reduces injuries and accessibility tools improve inclusion, then those benefits can offset the harms the opponent emphasizes in realistic safety deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace privacy/economic harms prevent AI from being beneficial across society.
objection: AI also improves health outcomes, education/work productivity, and accessibility, so workplace harms do not automatically eliminate broader welfare gains across society.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy harms do not prevent people from using AI-enabled health and education tools.
objection: Privacy harms reduce trust and willingness to share data, which can reduce engagement with AI-enabled health and education services and thereby cancel some of those benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that economic harms do not stop people from benefiting from AI.
objection: Economic instability and livelihood harm reduce people’s resources and ability to access health care, education, and support systems, which can cancel AI’s claimed benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that accessibility and work/education benefits reach marginalized groups despite discrimination harms.
objection: If AI intensifies racial discrimination through biased outputs and downstream effects, marginalized groups may receive worse or less appropriate outcomes, preventing the benefits from being realized for them.

target: AG1’s assumption that there is no evidence AI’s benefits are canceled by the harms it identified.
objection: Privacy, economic, and discrimination harms themselves provide evidence that AI’s benefits can be reduced, prevented, or canceled in practice by lowering uptake, access, and fair outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms necessarily arise even in safety-focused, restricted-access AI.
objection: The privacy harms described—such as loss of autonomy and manipulation through misuse—require detailed worker data to be broadly accessed, repurposed, or poorly secured; if safety AI is tightly restricted and secured, those harms need not materialize.

target: AG2’s claim that safety-focused AI is intrinsically net negative because of privacy harms.
objection: If serious privacy harms need not materialize in restricted safety-focused use, then the opponent’s premise that privacy harms persist in those deployments is not reliable.

target: AG2’s claim that economic harm is inevitable in workplace safety AI.
objection: Safety-focused AI can be used only for hazard detection and incident prevention, without being tied to labor replacement or cost-cutting workforce decisions, so economic livelihood harms are not inevitable.

target: AG1’s assumption that safety-only, restricted-access workplace AI avoids privacy harms.
objection: Even when data are used only for safety, collecting worker traces still monitors behavior and can itself cause surveillance, chilling, and autonomy harms.

target: AG1’s claim that serious privacy harms need not materialize in safety-focused deployments.
objection: Because privacy harms can arise from the monitoring itself, not just from repurposing or poor security, it is not generally true that such harms disappear in safety-focused restricted use.

target: AG2’s broader claim that AI’s core operation inherently creates severe harms that make it socially bad overall.
objection: AI can deliver substantial benefits in health, education, work, accessibility, and safety, and if those harms are not inevitable in well-governed or privacy-preserving deployments, AI can still be good for society overall.
